content: Hospital readmissions refer to the unplanned return of a patient to any acute care hospital within a specific time frame after being discharged from a prior hospitalization. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) focus on measuring unplanned readmissions within 30 days, as longer time frames (e.g., 90 days) may be influenced by factors outside the hospital's control, such as new illnesses, patient behavior, or post-discharge care. However, readmissions occurring within 2 days may hold greater clinical significance than those within 30 days. Approximately 6% of patients are readmitted within 30 days of discharge. A study of Medicare patients in the United States revealed that most variations in readmission rates are attributable to patient characteristics, with hospital or provider characteristics playing a smaller role. A systematic review estimated that about 25% of readmissions are avoidable, though individual studies showed wide variability in these rates. Physicians often use specific predictors for readmissions, but these predictors lack sensitivity. For example, having two or more hospitalizations within a year is a simple predictor of readmission. A study at the University of Pennsylvania Health System found that two or more inpatient admissions in the past 12 months had a sensitivity of 39% and a specificity of 84% for predicting readmissions. Approximately one-third of hospitalizations are considered preventable. Recent trials, however, have shown less impact in reducing readmissions. For instance, a virtual ward intervention reduced admissions by 4%, but this result was not statistically significant. Another trial involving an interprofessional intervention demonstrated some benefit, with about 50% of patients receiving a transition-of-care visit within 7 days. The CHAMP (Complex High Admission Management Program) trial in 2021 found no significant benefit, although both the intervention and control groups experienced some improvements. In this trial, 48% of intervention patients attended the CHAMP clinic at least once. The role of primary care coordination was not explicitly addressed in the trial. Prioritized rounds by inpatient physicians on the day of discharge did not affect the length of stay or discharge timing, but their impact on readmissions was not studied. Scripted telephone calls to patients after discharge may be effective. Discharge planning that includes coordination of post-discharge services may also help reduce readmissions. Medication reviews, when combined with other interventions, may lower readmission rates, though reviews conducted solely by the hospital team may not provide significant benefit. A Cochrane meta-analysis on medication reconciliation found no clear advantage. However, a Medicaid cohort study found that seeing a primary care provider within one week of discharge was beneficial. Among patients who already had a primary care physician, the impact of such visits was uncertain. The Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center demonstrated that interventions could increase outpatient follow-up visits after hospitalization (achieved in 60% of cases), but the effect on preventing readmissions remains unclear. A 2% drop in readmission rates was observed, but this was not statistically significant. Phone calls from primary care sites to patients after discharge may be helpful, and follow-up visits after emergency department visits could reduce disparities in readmissions. Team-based care has shown potential in reducing hospitalizations among veterans, though its effect on readmissions specifically was not studied. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP) has not demonstrated clear benefits. Similarly, the Camden Coalition's hotspotting model failed to reduce readmissions among high-utilization patients in a randomized controlled trial. Limitations of this study included low adherence to post-discharge follow-up visits, with home visits within 5 days and provider visits within 7 days achieved less than 30% of the time. Only 36% of patients saw a physician within 7 days of discharge. The TARGET-READ project was also unsuccessful, possibly due to its inability to increase primary care visits. Proactive and coordinated efforts by pharmacy teams during discharge planning may improve medication acquisition, as shown in a trial where 84% of intervention patients obtained their medications compared to 69% in the control group. Providing both verbal and written discharge instructions increased patients' healthcare-related knowledge at follow-up visits compared to verbal instructions alone (79% vs. 73%). Hospital consultation with outpatient clinicians for medically complex children may reduce readmissions and hospital length of stay.
